routes.what: Abram leaves Ur of the Chaldeans with his father Terah, settles in Harran, then goes on to Canaan, down to Egypt in a famine, and back to Hebron.
routes.note: The Bible gives no fixed date. Estimates run from about 2100 to 1800 BC; the slider uses 2000 BC.

routes.what: Israel leaves Egypt from Rameses, crosses the sea, receives the law at Mount Sinai, spends forty years in the wilderness and reaches the plains of Moab across the Jordan from Jericho. The stops follow the list in Numbers 33.
routes.note: Most stops have no confirmed site, and the route is argued over: a southern route to Jebel Musa (shown), a northern route along the coast, and routes to Arabia. The slider uses the early date from 1 Kings 6:1; many historians prefer about 1250 BC, and some doubt one single event.

routes.what: Assyria takes Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, and deports its people to Halah, to Gozan on the Habor river and to the cities of the Medes. Sargon II's own annals count 27,290 people taken.
routes.note: The text names where they were sent, not the road; the line joins the named places.

routes.what: Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon takes Jerusalem in 597 BC and again in 586 BC, burns the temple, brings King Zedekiah before him at Riblah and carries the people to Babylon.
routes.note: The road between the named places is the usual way round the Fertile Crescent, not given in the text (marked as a waypoint).

routes.what: After Persia takes Babylon, Cyrus lets the exiles go home. The first group returns under Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem.
routes.note: The Cyrus Cylinder records this policy for other peoples; it does not name the Jews. The road is the usual one, not given in the text.

routes.what: Born in Bethlehem, taken to Egypt, raised in Nazareth; baptised at the Jordan, ministry around Galilee from Capernaum, then the last journey through Jericho to Jerusalem, where he is crucified.
routes.note: The Gospels do not give one fixed order for the ministry. Birth is usually put at 6 to 4 BC and the crucifixion at AD 30 or 33; the slider uses AD 30.

routes.what: Paul and Barnabas are sent from Antioch to Cyprus and the cities of southern Asia Minor, then return the same way to Antioch.

Paul and Silas revisit the churches of Asia Minor, cross to Europe after a vision, found churches at Philippi, Thessalonica and Corinth (eighteen months there), and return by Ephesus, Caesarea and Jerusalem.
routes.note: The Gallio inscription at Delphi dates Paul's time in Corinth to about AD 50 to 52.

routes.what: Paul goes back through Galatia and Phrygia to Ephesus and stays about three years, then travels through Macedonia and Greece and sails home along the coast to Jerusalem, where he is arrested.
As a prisoner who has appealed to Caesar, Paul sails from Caesarea, is caught in a storm for fourteen days and wrecked on Malta, winters there and reaches Rome by Puteoli and the Appian Way.
The Persian king crosses the Hellespont on bridges of boats, marches round the north Aegean, forces the pass at Thermopylae, burns Athens and loses his fleet at Salamis.
routes.note: Herodotus's army figures (millions) are not believed; modern estimates are in the low hundreds of thousands at most.

routes.what: Alexander of Macedon crosses into Asia, beats the Persian armies at the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela, takes Egypt, Babylon and Persepolis, pushes on to Central Asia and the Indus, and dies at Babylon aged 32.

s.n: Hyphasis: the army refuses to go on

routes.what: Hannibal marches a Carthaginian army with elephants from Spain over the Pyrenees and the Alps into Italy, and destroys Roman armies at the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae.
routes.note: Which Alpine pass he used is one of history's oldest arguments (Traversette, Clapier, Mont Cenis, Little St Bernard and others); the crossing is drawn dashed.

routes.what: Julius Caesar turns back the Helvetii, crosses the Rhine and twice lands in Britain, then crushes the great Gallic revolt under Vercingetorix at the siege of Alesia.
routes.note: His own account; the Rhine bridge and the British landing places are not known exactly.

routes.what: Pope Urban II calls for an armed pilgrimage at Clermont. The armies gather at Constantinople, take Nicaea, win at Dorylaeum, besiege Antioch for eight months and take Jerusalem in July 1099 with a massacre of its people.

Batu and Subutai take Volga Bulgaria, sack Ryazan, Vladimir and Kyiv, and break the Hungarian army at Mohi; a second army wins at Legnica in Poland. They withdraw in 1242, after news of the Great Khan's death.

routes.n: The Mongol northern army in Poland
routes.what: A Mongol army under Orda and Baidar sweeps through Poland, burns Kraków and destroys a Polish and Silesian army at Legnica, then turns south to join Batu in Hungary.

The Grande Armée crosses the Niemen with about 422,000 men by Minard's count, wins at Borodino, takes a burning Moscow and retreats through the Russian winter. About 10,000 of the main column cross back.
routes.note: Troop numbers are Minard's own, the best-known chart of the campaign; other counts differ.

routes.what: After taking Atlanta, Union General William T. Sherman marches 62,000 men across Georgia to Savannah, living off the land and wrecking railways and farms, to break the South's will and supplies.

routes.n: World War II: D-Day to the Elbe
routes.what: Allied armies land in Normandy, break out in July, free Paris and Brussels, survive the German winter attack in the Ardennes, cross the Rhine at Remagen and meet the Soviet army on the Elbe at Torgau.
routes.note: This shows the line of advance through dated places, not the full front line.

routes.n: World War II: Stalingrad to Berlin
routes.what: The Soviet army destroys the German Sixth Army at Stalingrad, wins the tank battle at Kursk, retakes Kyiv, shatters Army Group Centre in Belarus and storms Berlin.
routes.note: This shows the line of advance through dated places, not the full front line.

routes.n: World War II in the Pacific
routes.what: From the attack on Pearl Harbor, through Midway and Guadalcanal, the US moves island by island across the Pacific to Leyte, Iwo Jima and Okinawa; atomic bombs fall on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and Japan surrenders in Tokyo Bay.
routes.note: This shows the line of advance through dated places, not the full front line.

routes.n: Out of Africa: to South Asia and Australia
routes.what: Modern humans spread out of Africa, probably across the mouth of the Red Sea and along the coasts of Arabia and India, reaching Southeast Asia and, by boat, Australia.
routes.note: A broad picture from ancient DNA and archaeology; the exact path and the dates (Australia between about 65,000 and 47,000 years ago) are debated.

routes.n: Out of Africa: to Europe and East Asia
routes.what: Another stream passes through the Levant into Europe, where people meet and mix with Neanderthals, and east across Asia to China.
routes.note: A broad picture from ancient DNA and archaeology; the dates are approximate.

routes.what: From the Near East people spread across Iran and Central Asia; a man buried at Ust'-Ishim in Siberia 45,000 years ago and the Tianyuan man near Beijing 40,000 years ago are among the oldest dated.
routes.note: A broad picture; the path between the dated finds is a guess.

routes.what: People from Siberia live on the land bridge of Beringia during the Ice Age, then move south, most likely down the Pacific coast, reaching southern Chile by about 14,500 years ago.
routes.note: When people first arrived is hotly debated. Footprints at White Sands, New Mexico are dated to about 23,000 to 21,000 years ago; some scholars question that date.

routes.what: Farmers and seafarers from Taiwan spread by outrigger canoe through the Philippines and Indonesia, then, as the Lapita people, out into the open Pacific as far as Tonga and Samoa.
routes.note: Dated by language family trees and archaeology; each date is approximate.

routes.what: After a pause of nearly 2,000 years in West Polynesia, voyagers settle the Society Islands and then, in a fast burst, the far corners of the Pacific, including Hawaiʻi.
routes.note: Radiocarbon dates from Wilmshurst and others (2011); earlier dates once proposed have not held up.

routes.what: Voyagers from central East Polynesia find Rapa Nui (Easter Island), one of the most remote inhabited places on Earth.
The last large land on Earth to be settled: Polynesian voyagers, ancestors of the Māori, reach Aotearoa from the Cook and Society Islands.

routes.n: Across the Indian Ocean to Madagascar
routes.what: Austronesian sailors from southern Borneo cross the Indian Ocean and settle Madagascar, where they mix with people from East Africa; Malagasy is still an Austronesian language.
routes.note: The route is not known; the line is a sketch.

routes.n: The Bantu expansion: the western stream
routes.what: Farming peoples speaking Bantu languages spread from the borderland of Nigeria and Cameroon through the rainforest along the Sangha river and south to Angola and Namibia.
routes.note: Dated from language trees and archaeology; each date is approximate.

routes.n: The Bantu expansion: the eastern stream
routes.what: Another stream reaches the Great Lakes, then the East African coast, and moves south to Mozambique and South Africa, bringing farming and iron working.
routes.note: Dated from language trees and archaeology; each date is approximate.

routes.what: Ancient DNA shows herders of the Yamnaya culture moving west from the Pontic steppe into Europe; their ancestry reaches Britain with the Beaker people.
routes.note: The movement of people is clear in DNA. Whether it brought the Indo-European languages to Europe is still argued (the steppe and Anatolian theories).

routes.what: Fleeing the Huns, Goths cross the Danube into the Roman Empire, destroy an emperor's army at Adrianople, sack Rome in 410 and are settled in south-west Gaul.

routes.n: The Norse cross the North Atlantic
routes.what: Norse settlers move from western Norway to the Faroes and Iceland, Erik the Red founds the Greenland colony, and his son Leif reaches North America. Tree rings at L'Anse aux Meadows show Norse cutting wood there in AD 1021.

The US Army forces about 16,000 Cherokee from their homes in the Southeast into camps and then west to Indian Territory (now Oklahoma). Thousands die in the camps and on the way; about 4,000 is the usual estimate.
routes.note: This is the northern land route most groups took; others went by river or by other roads.

routes.what: Driven out of Nauvoo, Illinois, members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints cross Iowa, winter on the Missouri, and the first company under Brigham Young reaches the Salt Lake Valley on 24 July 1847.
About 1,000 settlers leave Independence, Missouri in May 1843 and reach the Willamette Valley by November. Some 300,000 to 400,000 people use the trail before the railways.

routes.n: Atlantic slave trade: West Central Africa to Brazil
routes.what: Across the whole trade about 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships and about 10.7 million survived the crossing. West Central Africa (Luanda, Benguela) to Brazil was the largest single flow.
routes.note: Lines show the main flows between regions, not single voyages; the database lists more than 36,000 voyages.

routes.n: Atlantic slave trade: Bight of Benin to Bahia
routes.what: Captives sold at Ouidah and other ports of the Bight of Benin were carried mostly to Bahia in Brazil and to the Caribbean.
routes.note: Lines show the main flows between regions, not single voyages.

routes.n: Atlantic slave trade: Gold Coast to the Caribbean
routes.what: From the forts of the Gold Coast, such as Elmina and Cape Coast, ships carried captives mainly to Jamaica, Barbados and the other Caribbean colonies.
routes.note: Lines show the main flows between regions, not single voyages.

routes.n: Atlantic slave trade: Bight of Biafra and Senegambia to North America
routes.what: About 400,000 of the people carried across the Atlantic were landed in mainland North America, many of them from the Bight of Biafra and Senegambia to Charleston and the Chesapeake.
routes.note: Lines show the main flows between regions, not single voyages.

routes.n: The Great Migration: Mississippi to Chicago
routes.what: About 6 million Black Americans leave the rural South for cities in the North and West, escaping segregation and violence and seeking work. The Illinois Central railroad carried many from Mississippi to Chicago.

routes.n: The Great Migration: Alabama to Detroit
routes.what: Many from Alabama and Tennessee go north to the car factories of Detroit.

routes.n: The Great Migration: the Carolinas and Georgia to New York
routes.what: From the Atlantic coast states people go north to Philadelphia, New York and Harlem.

routes.n: The Great Migration: Texas and Louisiana to California
routes.what: In the second wave, from the 1940s, many from Texas and Louisiana go west to the shipyards and factories of Los Angeles and Oakland.

When British India is split into India and Pakistan, Hindus and Sikhs flee west Punjab for India and Muslims flee east Punjab for Pakistan. About 14 million people move, and hundreds of thousands, perhaps a million, are killed.

routes.n: Partition of India: to West Pakistan
routes.what: Muslims from Delhi and east Punjab travel to Lahore and on to Karachi, by foot, cart and refugee trains.
Bengal is also split: Hindus leave East Pakistan (now Bangladesh) for West Bengal, and many Muslims go the other way, over several years.

A web of caravan routes linking Han China with Central Asia, Persia and the Roman world. Silk, paper and spices went west; horses, glass, silver, religions and ideas moved too. Almost no one travelled the whole way.
routes.note: One main line of a wide network. Zhang Qian's missions (138 to 126 BC) opened it to Han China.

routes.n: The Silk Road: southern Tarim branch
routes.what: The southern road skirted the Taklamakan desert through the oasis towns of Loulan and Khotan, famous for its jade.
Camel caravans carried frankincense and myrrh from southern Arabia north through the desert to Petra and the Mediterranean port of Gaza. The Nabataeans of Petra grew rich on it.
Roman traders bought Baltic amber and carried it south along the river valleys to Carnuntum on the Danube and down to Aquileia on the Adriatic, where it was carved.

routes.n: Across the Sahara: gold and salt
routes.what: Caravans of thousands of camels linked North Africa with the gold fields of West Africa. Salt from the mines of Taghaza was traded for gold at Walata and Timbuktu, the wealth behind the empires of Ghana, Mali and Songhay.

routes.n: Across the Sahara: Tripoli to Kano
routes.what: The eastern road ran from Tripoli through the Fezzan and the salt oasis of Bilma to Kanem-Bornu and the Hausa cities such as Kano. It carried enslaved people north as well as goods.

routes.n: Rome to India by the monsoon
routes.what: Greek and Egyptian merchants sailed from the Red Sea port of Berenike to India on the summer monsoon and back on the winter one, trading Roman gold and wine for pepper, pearls, cotton and silk.

For 250 years Spanish galleons crossed the Pacific once or twice a year, bringing Mexican and Peruvian silver to Manila for Chinese silk and porcelain: the first trade route to link the Americas and Asia.

Three ships leave Palos, refit in the Canary Islands, and after 33 days at sea reach an island the Taíno call Guanahani. Columbus explores Cuba and Hispaniola, loses the Santa María, and sails home believing he has reached Asia.
routes.note: Which island was Guanahani is still debated (San Salvador is most often named; Samana Cay is another candidate).

routes.n: Vasco da Gama sails to India
routes.what: Four Portuguese ships swing far out into the South Atlantic, round the Cape of Good Hope, follow the East African coast to Malindi, and with a local pilot cross to Calicut: the first sea route from Europe to India.

routes.n: Magellan and Elcano: around the world
routes.what: Five ships and about 270 men leave Spain to reach the Spice Islands by sailing west. They find the strait at the tip of South America and cross the Pacific; Magellan is killed at Mactan. Juan Sebastián Elcano brings the Victoria home with 18 men, the first voyage around the world.

The Ming admiral's treasure fleet, the largest of its age, sails from Nanjing through Southeast Asia to Calicut and Hormuz; parts of the fleet visit Mecca and East Africa. Zheng He dies on the way home.
routes.note: Dates follow the itinerary kept by Zhu Yunming, as given in Mills's edition of Ma Huan.

routes.what: A young scholar from Tangier sets out on the pilgrimage to Mecca and keeps travelling for 29 years, about 120,000 km across the Islamic world: Arabia, East Africa, Central Asia, India, the Maldives, China and Mali.
routes.note: Dates are from his own account and are often loose; some scholars doubt parts of his China and Central Asia journeys (drawn dashed).

routes.what: The Corps of Discovery rows up the Missouri, winters with the Mandan, where Sacagawea joins them, crosses the Rockies on foot and horseback and canoes down the Columbia to the Pacific, then returns to St Louis.

events.what: Ramesses II of Egypt fights the Hittite king Muwatalli II near Kadesh on the Orontes, one of the largest chariot battles known. Both sides claimed victory; their later treaty is the oldest known peace treaty.
The Athenians and Plataeans defeat a Persian landing force on the plain of Marathon.
Octavian's fleet defeats Antony and Cleopatra off western Greece; Octavian becomes Augustus, first Roman emperor.
Germanic tribes under Arminius destroy three Roman legions under Varus. Rome gives up conquering Germany east of the Rhine.
Roman legions under Titus break into Jerusalem and burn the Second Temple, ending the great Jewish revolt.
Charles Martel's Franks defeat an Umayyad army from Spain between Tours and Poitiers.
William of Normandy defeats and kills King Harold II and takes the English throne.
Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II takes Constantinople after a 53-day siege, ending the Byzantine Empire.
Wellington's allied army and Blücher's Prussians defeat Napoleon for the last time.
Three days of fighting end Lee's invasion of the North; about 51,000 killed, wounded, captured or missing on both sides.
British and French armies attack on the Somme; the British lose 57,470 men on the first day. By November over a million on all sides are killed or wounded.
Human footprints in an old lake bed dated by seeds to about 23,000 to 21,000 years ago, which would put people in North America during the height of the Ice Age. Some scholars question the dating.
